tests.title: SAT Practice Test 1
tests.description: Full-length digital SAT style practice test (sample core content).

questions.passage: Marine biologists have long assumed that the deep sea, far from sunlight, supports little plant life. Recent expeditions, however, have documented algae mats thriving near hydrothermal vents, where chemical energy substitutes for the light that surface plants require.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that hydrothermal vents are dangerous to marine life
To describe an unexpected finding that challenges a prior assumption
To compare deep-sea algae with surface algae in detail
To explain how sunlight reaches the deep sea

questions.passage: The novelist revised her manuscript seven times, insisting that each draft revealed flaws invisible in the last. Critics later praised the finished novel for its ______ prose, unaware of the labor behind its apparent ease.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
options: effortless
chaotic
unfinished
predictable

questions.passage: Data from a 2023 transit study: Bus ridership rose 12% after fare-free days were introduced, while subway ridership rose only 3% over the same period, despite both systems serving similar neighborhoods.
questions.prompt: Which statement is most strongly supported by the data?
options: Fare-free days had a larger effect on bus ridership than on subway ridership.
Subway ridership fell after fare-free days were introduced.
Bus and subway ridership rose by identical amounts.
Fare-free days had no measurable effect on ridership.

questions.passage: Although the committee approved the budget unanimously, several members privately expressed reservations about its long-term sustainability.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole? ("privately expressed reservations")
options: It shows that the committee's public vote concealed private disagreement.
It proves the budget was rejected.
It shows that all members were fully confident in the budget.
It is irrelevant to the committee's decision.

questions.prompt: If 3x + 7 = 22, what is the value of x?
A line passes through the points (0, 4) and (2, 10). What is the slope of the line?
The perimeter of a square is 36. What is the area of the square? (Enter a numeric value.)
If f(x) = 2x^2 - 3, what is f(3)? (Enter a numeric value.)

practiceQuestions.title: The comma splice that looks right
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: proposal, it
proposal; it
proposal it
proposal, it,
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both halves are independent clauses. A semicolon can join them; a comma alone creates a comma splice.
practiceQuestions.passage: The committee reviewed the ______ approved the final version after lunch.
rationales: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
Correct. A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
No punctuation creates a run-on sentence.
Still a comma splice, plus an extra comma between the subject "it" and its verb.

steps.title: Find the clauses
steps.body: "The committee reviewed the proposal" and "it approved the final version" can each stand alone.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.body: Two independent clauses need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus FANBOYS.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: approved the final version after lunch
practiceQuestions.hint: Could each side of the blank be its own sentence?

practiceQuestions.title: What the study actually suggests
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly strengthen the researchers' conclusion?
options: The neighborhoods planted their trees at different times.
Residents prefer the appearance of mature trees.
Tree-rich neighborhoods have higher property values.
Temperatures in all the neighborhoods were measured at the same time of day and at the same elevation.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Measuring at the same time and elevation rules out other explanations, so the temperature difference is more plausibly caused by the trees.
practiceQuestions.passage: A study finds that neighborhoods with more mature trees report cooler summer temperatures than neighborhoods with fewer trees. The researchers conclude that the trees themselves cause the cooler temperatures.
rationales: Planting times don't help show that the trees cause cooling.
Residents' preferences are irrelevant to temperature.
Property values are a different variable; if anything they suggest other differences between neighborhoods.
Correct. Controlling time of day and elevation removes other possible causes, which strengthens the causal claim.

steps.title: Pin down the claim
steps.body: The claim is causal: trees cause cooler temperatures.
steps.quote: the trees themselves cause the cooler temperatures

steps.title: Ask what could weaken it
steps.body: Other differences, such as when or where temperatures were measured, could explain the gap.

steps.title: Pick the choice that rules those out
steps.body: D controls for time and elevation, making the trees the most plausible cause.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: The researchers conclude that the trees themselves cause the cooler temperatures.
practiceQuestions.hint: To strengthen a cause-and-effect claim, rule out other possible causes.

practiceQuestions.title: Precision over personality
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: ambiguous
irrelevant
tentative
corroborating
practiceQuestions.explanation: Independent experiments producing the same result confirm one another, so the evidence is corroborating.
practiceQuestions.passage: The evidence was ______: several independent experiments produced the same result.
rationales: Consistent results are the opposite of ambiguous.
Nothing suggests the evidence is off-topic.
Repeated confirmation makes evidence stronger, not tentative.
Correct. "Corroborating" means confirming, which is what repeated independent results do.

steps.title: Use the colon
steps.body: Everything after the colon explains the blank.
steps.quote: several independent experiments produced the same result

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: several independent experiments produced the same result
practiceQuestions.hint: The part after the colon defines the blank.

practiceQuestions.title: The contrast signal
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: However,
Similarly,
For example,
Therefore,
practiceQuestions.explanation: The second sentence contradicts the city's expectation, so a contrast transition is needed.
practiceQuestions.passage: The city expected its new bike lanes to be used mostly on weekends. ______ weekday commuters accounted for 70% of all trips.
rationales: Correct. Expected weekends, but actually weekdays: a contrast.
"Similarly" signals agreement, but the sentences conflict.
The second sentence isn't an example of the first.
The second sentence isn't a consequence of the first.

steps.title: Cover the choices
steps.body: Read both sentences on their own.

steps.title: Name the relationship
steps.quote: expected its new bike lanes to be used mostly on weekends

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: The city expected its new bike lanes to be used mostly on weekends.
practiceQuestions.hint: Does the second sentence agree with the first, or surprise you?

practiceQuestions.title: The distracting prepositional phrase
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: are
were
have been
is
practiceQuestions.explanation: The subject is the singular "collection," not "manuscripts"; "now" calls for the present tense.
practiceQuestions.passage: The collection of rare manuscripts, gathered over four decades by the library's founders, ______ now available online.
rationales: "Are" is plural; the subject "collection" is singular.
"Were" is plural and past tense.
"Have been" is plural.
Correct. Singular subject + present tense ("now") → "is."

steps.title: Cross out the extras
steps.body: Remove "of rare manuscripts" and the phrase between the commas.
steps.quote: The collection ... now available online.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: The collection of rare manuscripts
practiceQuestions.hint: What is actually available online: the collection, or the manuscripts?

practiceQuestions.title: Main idea in one line
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Honeybees prefer to forage close to their hives.
Researchers have trained bees to dance on command.
Bee dances encode information that researchers can use to study foraging.
The waggle dance is the only way bees communicate.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The text explains what the dance encodes and how researchers use it. Choice C captures both parts without overreaching.
practiceQuestions.passage: Honeybees perform a "waggle dance" whose angle and duration tell other bees the direction and distance of food. Researchers who have learned to decode these dances have used them to map where colonies forage across entire seasons.
rationales: The text never says how far bees prefer to fly, so this adds a claim the passage doesn't make.
Researchers decode the dances; nothing suggests they trained bees to perform them.
Correct. The first sentence says what the dance encodes; the second says researchers use it to map foraging. C combines both.
"The only way" is extreme. The text describes one form of communication without ruling out others.

steps.title: Summarize each sentence
steps.body: Sentence 1: the dance tells other bees where food is. Sentence 2: researchers decode it to map foraging.

steps.title: Combine them into one idea
steps.body: The dance carries information, and scientists can use that information.
steps.quote: used them to map where colonies forage across entire seasons

steps.title: Check the choices
steps.body: Only C covers both halves. A and D add claims the text doesn't make, and B misreads who does what.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: have used them to map where colonies forage across entire seasons
practiceQuestions.hint: The main idea should cover both sentences, not just the first.

practiceQuestions.title: Data that actually supports the claim
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student's claim?
options: Students said they enjoyed the program.
Scores rose 15% for program participants but stayed flat for similar students who did not participate.
The program was expensive to run.
Reading scores rose at many schools nationwide in the same year.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A comparison group that didn't improve isolates the program's effect.
practiceQuestions.passage: A student claims that a school's new reading program improved students' reading scores.
rationales: Enjoyment says nothing about whether scores improved.
Correct. Participants improved while similar non-participants didn't, which points to the program as the cause.
Cost is irrelevant to whether the program worked.
A nationwide rise suggests something other than this program raised scores, which weakens the claim.

steps.title: Restate the claim
steps.body: The program caused higher reading scores.

steps.title: Think like a scientist
steps.body: The strongest support compares students who got the program with similar students who didn't.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: a school's new reading program improved students' reading scores
practiceQuestions.hint: What kind of comparison would show the program, not something else, made the difference?

practiceQuestions.title: Colon before a list
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: essentials;
essentials, and
essentials:
essentials
practiceQuestions.explanation: A colon introduces a list after a complete independent clause.
practiceQuestions.passage: The expedition carried three ______ water filters, satellite phones, and spare batteries.
rationales: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides; the list isn't one.
"And" makes the list sound like extra items rather than the three essentials.
Correct. "The expedition carried three essentials" is complete, so a colon can introduce the list.
No punctuation runs "essentials" straight into the list, which is ungrammatical.

steps.title: Check the first part
steps.body: "The expedition carried three essentials" is a complete clause.

steps.title: Check the second part
steps.body: A list that names the three essentials.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: water filters, satellite phones, and spare batteries
practiceQuestions.hint: What punctuation introduces a list after a complete sentence?

practiceQuestions.title: Meet the goal, not the notes
practiceQuestions.prompt: The student wants to emphasize a difference in the kinds of light the two telescopes observe. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Hubble and Webb are both space telescopes.
While Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light, Webb observes mainly infrared light.
Webb launched in 2021, many years after Hubble.
Both telescopes have produced famous images.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only B contrasts the kinds of light ("While ... "), which is exactly the goal.
practiceQuestions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990.
• Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
• The James Webb Space Telescope launched in 2021.
• Webb observes mainly infrared light.
rationales: This is a similarity, not a difference.
Correct. "While" sets up the contrast, and it names each telescope's kind of light.
This is a difference, but in launch dates, not in the light observed.
A similarity, and it isn't in the notes.

steps.title: Read the goal first
steps.body: A difference in the kinds of light observed.
steps.quote: emphasize a difference in the kinds of light the two telescopes observe

steps.title: Filter the choices
steps.body: Drop similarities (A, D) and differences about something else (C).

steps.title: Choose
steps.body: B is the only choice that contrasts the light.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light
practiceQuestions.hint: Read the goal carefully: a difference in what, exactly?

practiceQuestions.title: Hard to find fault
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: verbose
cogent
cursory
polemical
practiceQuestions.explanation: Critics couldn't fault the reasoning, so the speech was clear and convincing: cogent.
practiceQuestions.passage: The senator's speech was so ______ that even her critics admitted it was difficult to find fault with its reasoning.
rationales: "Verbose" (wordy) wouldn't make the reasoning hard to criticize.
Correct. "Cogent" means clear, logical, and convincing, which explains why critics couldn't find fault.
"Cursory" (hasty, superficial) would make the reasoning easier to criticize.
"Polemical" (aggressively argumentative) doesn't explain why critics agreed.

steps.title: Find the result
steps.body: The "so ... that" structure means the blank caused the result.
steps.quote: even her critics admitted it was difficult to find fault with its reasoning

steps.title: Predict
steps.body: The speech was very convincing and logical.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: even her critics admitted it was difficult to find fault with its reasoning
practiceQuestions.hint: The blank must cause even critics to agree.

practiceQuestions.title: Whose supplies?
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: they're
their
there
its
practiceQuestions.explanation: "Their" is the plural possessive pronoun, matching "volunteers."
practiceQuestions.passage: The volunteers brought ______ own supplies to the cleanup.
rationales: "They're" means "they are."
Correct. Plural possessive for the plural "volunteers."
"There" refers to a place.
"Its" is singular and isn't used for people.

steps.title: What's needed
steps.body: A possessive: the supplies belong to the volunteers.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: The volunteers brought
practiceQuestions.hint: The supplies belong to whom? One person or many?

practiceQuestions.title: Then and now
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a problem and then a solution.
It describes a process step by step.
It contrasts an early reaction with a later one.
It lists examples supporting one claim.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The text moves from how the work was received then to how it is received now: a contrast over time.
practiceQuestions.passage: Early critics dismissed the painter's work as unfinished. Today, museums compete to display it.
rationales: No problem is solved; opinions simply changed.
No process is described.
Correct. "Early critics" and "Today" frame a contrast between two reactions.
The two sentences contrast; they don't both support one claim.

steps.title: Label each sentence
steps.body: Sentence 1: early rejection. Sentence 2: current enthusiasm.

steps.title: Name the relationship
steps.body: Time words ("Early," "Today") mark a before-and-after contrast.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: Today, museums compete to display it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Notice the time words at the start of each sentence.

practiceQuestions.title: A line through two points
practiceQuestions.prompt: A line passes through (2, 5) and (6, 13). What is its slope?
rationales: This is run ÷ rise (4 ÷ 8). Slope is rise ÷ run.
4 is the change in x (the run), not the slope.
8 is the change in y (the rise). Divide it by the run.
practiceQuestions.hint: Slope = (change in y) ÷ (change in x).

practiceQuestions.title: The quadratic in disguise
practiceQuestions.prompt: If x² − 7x + 12 = 0 and x > 3, what is the value of x?
practiceQuestions.explanation: x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 4), so x = 3 or x = 4. Since x > 3, x = 4.
rationales: 2 doesn't satisfy the equation: 4 − 14 + 12 = 2, not 0.
3 is a solution, but the question requires x > 3.
Correct. The solutions are 3 and 4, and only 4 is greater than 3.
6 doesn't satisfy the equation: 36 − 42 + 12 = 6, not 0.

steps.title: Factor
steps.body:
Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to −7: −3 and −4.
(x − 3)(x − 4) = 0

practiceQuestions.hint: Factor the quadratic, then use the condition x > 3.

practiceQuestions.title: Percent increase on a price
practiceQuestions.prompt: A price increases from $80 to $100. What is the percent increase?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Increase = $20. Percent increase = 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25 = 25%. Always divide by the original value.
rationales: This divides the $20 increase by the new price, $100. Percent change divides by the original, $80.
80% is the old price as a percent of the new price.
125% is the new price as a percent of the old price, not the increase.
practiceQuestions.hint: Percent change = change ÷ original value.

practiceQuestions.title: Add the equations
practiceQuestions.prompt: If x + y = 10 and x − y = 4, what is the value of x?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Add the equations: 2x = 14, so x = 7 (and y = 3).
rationales: 3 is the value of y.
6 is 10 − 4, which is 2y, not x.
Correct. Adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7.
14 is 2x. Divide by 2.
practiceQuestions.hint: Adding the two equations makes y disappear.

practiceQuestions.title: Reading a function
practiceQuestions.prompt: A gym charges a $25 sign-up fee plus $15 per month. Which function gives the total cost C, in dollars, after m months?
options: C = 40m
practiceQuestions.explanation: The $15 is charged each month (slope) and the $25 is charged once (intercept): C = 15m + 25.
rationales: This swaps the monthly rate and the one-time fee.
Correct. $15 per month times m, plus the one-time $25.
This charges the $25 fee every month.
The sign-up fee adds to the cost; it isn't subtracted.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which amount repeats every month, and which is paid once?

practiceQuestions.title: Right triangle shortcut
practiceQuestions.prompt: A right triangle has legs of length 6 and 8. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, and √100 = 10 (a scaled 3-4-5 triangle).
rationales: Correct. 6² + 8² = 100, and √100 = 10.
12 doesn't satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 6² + 8² ≠ 12².
14 is 6 + 8. The theorem adds squares, not lengths.
48 is 6 × 8 (twice the area), not a side length.
practiceQuestions.hint: a² + b² = c². Or recognize a multiple of 3-4-5.

practiceQuestions.title: The mean of a data set
practiceQuestions.prompt: The data set 4, 7, 9, 10, x has a mean of 8. What is x?
rationales: The missing value doesn't have to equal the mean.
With x = 9 the sum would be 39, and 39 ÷ 5 = 7.8.
Correct. The total must be 40, and the known values add to 30.
With x = 12 the sum would be 42, and 42 ÷ 5 = 8.4.
practiceQuestions.hint: Mean × number of values = total.

practiceQuestions.title: Exponent rules
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which expression is equivalent to (x³)² · x⁴?
options: x⁹
x¹⁰
x²⁴
x¹²
practiceQuestions.explanation: (x³)² = x⁶, and x⁶ · x⁴ = x¹⁰.
rationales: This adds all three exponents (3 + 2 + 4). A power of a power multiplies.
Correct. (x³)² = x⁶, then x⁶ · x⁴ = x¹⁰.
This multiplies all three exponents. Multiplying powers with the same base adds exponents.
This multiplies 3 by (2 + 2); the 4 belongs to a separate factor.
practiceQuestions.hint: Power of a power: multiply exponents. Product of powers: add them.

practiceQuestions.title: Complete the square
practiceQuestions.prompt: The circle x² + y² − 6x + 4y = 12 has what radius?
rationales: √12 uses the constant before completing the square.
Correct. After completing the square, r² = 25, so r = 5.
25 is r², not r.
13 is 9 + 4, the constants added while completing the square, without the 12.
practiceQuestions.hint: Complete the square for x and y, then compare with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².

practiceQuestions.title: Scale up the recipe
practiceQuestions.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of sugar. How many cups of flour are needed with 8 cups of sugar?
options: 5⅓
practiceQuestions.explanation: 8 cups of sugar is 4 × 2, so flour = 4 × 3 = 12 cups.
rationales: This flips the ratio (8 × 2/3). Keep flour : sugar = 3 : 2.
This adds 6 to the flour because 6 was added to the sugar. Ratios scale by multiplying.
Correct. The sugar is multiplied by 4, so the flour is too: 3 × 4 = 12.
This doubles the sugar amount instead of using the ratio.
practiceQuestions.hint: How many times bigger is 8 than 2?

practiceQuestions.title: Doubling time
practiceQuestions.prompt: A bacteria population doubles every 3 hours. Starting from 500, which expression gives the population after t hours?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The number of doublings in t hours is t/3, so P = 500 · 2^(t/3).
rationales: This doubles 3 times every hour instead of once every 3 hours.
Correct. There are t/3 doublings in t hours.
This swaps the factor (2) and the doubling time (3).
This is linear growth. Doubling is exponential.

steps.title: Count the doublings
steps.body: One doubling every 3 hours → t/3 doublings in t hours.

practiceQuestions.hint: How many 3-hour periods are there in t hours?

practiceQuestions.title: Flip the sign
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which value of x satisfies −2x + 5 > 11?
practiceQuestions.explanation: −2x > 6 → x < −3 (dividing by a negative flips the sign). Only −4 is less than −3.
rationales: Correct. The inequality simplifies to x < −3, and −4 < −3.
At x = −3 both sides are equal, and the inequality is strict.
0 is not less than −3.
This comes from forgetting to flip the sign (x > −3 would allow 3).
practiceQuestions.hint: What happens to the inequality sign when you divide by a negative number?

practiceQuestions.title: The neighborhood farm
practiceQuestions.passage: In 2019, a group of residents in Detroit converted three vacant lots into a community farm. Within two years, the farm was supplying vegetables to a nearby school cafeteria and hosting weekend workshops on composting and seed saving. Organizers say the project's greatest success, however, has been social: neighbors who had never spoken now share tools, trade harvests, and meet regularly to plan the next season.
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A farm built on vacant lots has provided food and education, but organizers value most how it has connected neighbors.
Community farms in Detroit grow more vegetables than local schools can use.
Composting workshops are the most popular activity at the farm.
Residents built the farm because a local school asked for fresh vegetables.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The passage lists the farm's practical benefits, then uses "however" to stress that its greatest success is social.
rationales: Correct. A keeps the practical benefits and the text's emphasis on the social connection that organizers value most.
The text says the farm supplies a school cafeteria, not that it produces more than schools can use.
Workshops are mentioned, but nothing says they are the most popular activity.
The text never gives a reason the farm was started, so this cause is invented.

steps.title: Summarize the text
steps.body: Residents build a farm; it supplies food and runs workshops; organizers say its biggest success is social.

steps.title: Find the emphasis
steps.body: "However" signals the point the author cares about most.
steps.quote: the project's greatest success, however, has been social

steps.title: Match the choice
steps.body: A includes the benefits and the social emphasis. The other choices add claims or focus on a single detail.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: Organizers say the project's greatest success, however, has been social
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for the word that signals what matters most to the organizers.

practiceQuestions.title: The orchid's single partner
practiceQuestions.passage: Most flowering plants attract many kinds of pollinators, but the Australian hammer orchid depends on just one: a species of thynnid wasp. The orchid's lip mimics the shape and scent of a female wasp, luring males that try to carry it away. As a male grips the lip and attempts to fly, a hinge swings him into the flower's column, where pollen sticks to his back. Because the orchid relies on this single deception, it can reproduce only where that wasp species also lives.
practiceQuestions.prompt: According to the text, why can the hammer orchid reproduce only in certain places?
options: It needs a type of soil found only in parts of Australia.
Its flowers open only during the short season when wasps are active.
Female wasps destroy the flowers in areas where male wasps are rare.
It depends on a single wasp species for pollination, so it is limited to where that wasp lives.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The last sentence states the reason directly: the orchid relies on one wasp species, so it can reproduce only where that wasp lives.
rationales: Soil is never mentioned in the text.
The text says nothing about when the flowers open.
The orchid mimics female wasps; nothing says real female wasps harm the flowers.
Correct. The final sentence gives exactly this cause and effect.

steps.title: Identify the question
steps.body: It asks for a reason: why is reproduction limited to certain places?
steps.quote: why can the hammer orchid reproduce only in certain places?

steps.title: Find the line that answers it
steps.body: The last sentence begins with "Because" and states the limitation.
steps.quote: Because the orchid relies on this single deception, it can reproduce only where that wasp species also lives.

steps.title: Match it
steps.body: Choice D restates that sentence. The others bring in soil, seasons, or behavior the text never describes.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: Because the orchid relies on this single deception, it can reproduce only where that wasp species also lives.
practiceQuestions.hint: Detail questions are answered by one specific sentence. Which sentence contains "only where"?

practiceQuestions.title: The underrated translator
practiceQuestions.passage: When the first English translation of a celebrated Russian novel appeared in the 1880s, reviewers praised its energy and clarity but rarely mentioned its translator, Harriet Vale. Vale had worked mainly from a French version of the novel rather than the Russian original, and later scholars often faulted her for it. Yet her recently catalogued letters show that she checked difficult passages against the Russian with the help of native speakers, a practice suggesting that her translation was more careful than its reputation implies.
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Vale's translation was praised mainly because it was based on the Russian original.
Although Vale's translation has been criticized, new evidence suggests she worked on it more carefully than critics assumed.
Translations made from French versions of Russian novels are always unreliable.
Vale was the first translator to consult native speakers when translating Russian literature.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The text moves from criticism of Vale to evidence that complicates it: her letters show a careful process.
rationales: The text says she worked mainly from a French version, so this contradicts it.
Correct. B captures the shift from criticism ("faulted her") to the new evidence ("more careful than its reputation implies").
"Always unreliable" is a sweeping claim the text never makes.
The text never claims she was the first to do this.

steps.title: Track the turn
steps.body: The word "Yet" marks the author's main point, after the background and the criticism.

steps.title: Read the conclusion
steps.body: The final clause states what the letters suggest.
steps.quote: her translation was more careful than its reputation implies

steps.title: Choose the full summary
steps.body: B mentions both the criticism and the evidence that answers it. The others misstate or exaggerate details.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: a practice suggesting that her translation was more careful than its reputation implies
practiceQuestions.hint: The main idea usually comes after a turn word like "Yet" or "However".

practiceQuestions.title: Songs in a noisy city
practiceQuestions.passage: Researchers have found that great tits living in noisy cities sing at higher pitches than those in quiet forests. Because traffic noise is concentrated at low frequencies, a higher song is less likely to be drowned out. The shift may carry a cost, though: in some populations, females respond more strongly to lower-pitched songs, which they may associate with larger, healthier males. City birds, in other words, may be trading attractiveness for audibility.
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Female great tits in cities prefer males that sing at higher pitches than forest birds do.
Traffic noise has caused great tit populations in cities to shrink.
City great tits sing higher to be heard over traffic, but this may make their songs less appealing to potential mates.
Larger great tits always sing at lower pitches than smaller great tits.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The text describes an adaptation (higher songs) and its possible cost (less attractive to females), summed up in the last sentence.
rationales: The text says some females respond more to lower songs, the opposite of this choice.
Nothing in the text discusses population size.
Correct. C combines the benefit (audibility) and the cost (attractiveness) that the last sentence sums up.
The text says females may associate low songs with larger males; it never says larger birds always sing lower.

steps.title: Find the benefit
steps.body: Higher songs are harder for low-frequency traffic noise to mask.

steps.title: Find the cost
steps.body: Females in some populations prefer lower songs.
steps.quote: females respond more strongly to lower-pitched songs

steps.title: Use the summary sentence
steps.body: "In other words" introduces the author's own summary of the main idea.
steps.quote: City birds, in other words, may be trading attractiveness for audibility.

practiceQuestions.keyQuote: City birds, in other words, may be trading attractiveness for audibility.
practiceQuestions.hint: "In other words" often introduces the author's own summary.

practiceQuestions.title: A library of things
practiceQuestions.passage: Some public libraries now lend far more than books. The Sacramento Public Library, for example, runs a "Library of Things" where cardholders can borrow sewing machines, musical instruments, and board games. practiceQuestions.title: Free shipping math
practiceQuestions.passage: An online retailer began offering free shipping on all orders over $35. Because shipping costs per order also stayed about the same, the analysts concluded that the policy most likely ______
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: reduced the retailer's shipping costs per order.
attracted many new customers who had never shopped with the retailer.
increased the retailer's total sales without increasing the number of shipments it paid for.
caused customers to place more frequent small orders.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Same number of orders at a larger average size means more total sales, while shipments (one per order) stayed the same.
rationales: The text says shipping costs per order stayed about the same.
The number of orders didn't change, so there's no evidence of many new customers.

steps.body: A, B, and D each contradict one of the stated facts.

Star counts are never discussed.

practiceQuestions.title: Is breakfast the key?
practiceQuestions.passage:
Text 1
Many nutrition researchers argue that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. They point to studies showing that people who eat breakfast tend to have healthier body weights than people who skip it, and they conclude that eating breakfast helps people control their weight.

Text 2
Studies linking breakfast to healthy weight are mostly observational: they compare people who happen to eat breakfast with people who don't. Such people may differ in many other ways, such as how much they exercise. When researchers randomly assigned participants to eat or skip breakfast, the groups' weight changes were nearly identical.
practiceQuestions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion of the researchers in Text 1?

By claiming that people who skip breakfast exercise more than people who eat it
By insisting that observational studies of diet are always inaccurate
By arguing that the evidence they cite doesn't show that eating breakfast causes weight control
practiceQuestions.explanation: Text 2 says the Text 1 evidence is observational and that a randomized experiment found no difference, so it challenges the causal conclusion.
rationales: Text 2's experiment found no weight difference, so it would not agree.
Text 2 says the groups "may differ" in exercise; it doesn't claim which group exercises more.
"Always inaccurate" is too extreme; Text 2 only says observational studies can't isolate the cause.
Correct. Text 2 questions whether breakfast causes weight control, since the observational data can't show that and the experiment found no effect.

steps.title: Text 1's claim
steps.body: Breakfast helps control weight, based on comparisons of eaters and skippers.
steps.quote: they conclude that eating breakfast helps people control their weight

steps.title: Text 2's claim
steps.body: Those studies are observational; a randomized test showed no difference.

practiceQuestions.title: Steam and the mill towns
practiceQuestions.passage:

Text 2
Records from Lancashire mills complicate the steam-engine story. As late as the 1830s, water wheels still powered a substantial share of the region's cotton mills, and many early steam-powered mills were built along rivers anyway, because their boilers needed a reliable supply of water. practiceQuestions.title: Shrink the margin of error
practiceQuestions.prompt: Researchers surveyed a random sample of customers of a grocery chain and reported an estimate with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which change to the survey would most likely produce a smaller margin of error?

Surveying a smaller random sample of customers of a grocery chain
Reporting the results as fractions instead of percents
Surveying only customers who volunteer to respond online
rationales: Correct. Larger random samples produce less sampling variability, so the margin of error shrinks.
Smaller samples vary more, so the margin of error grows.
How results are written doesn't change their precision.
A voluntary sample introduces bias and doesn't reduce sampling error.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Margin of error shrinks as the size of a random sample grows.

steps.title: Recall the idea
steps.body: Margin of error measures how much a random sample's result could differ from the population value.

steps.title: What reduces it
steps.body: More data from a random sample means less chance variation.

steps.title: Eliminate
steps.body: Smaller or biased samples don't help, and formatting doesn't matter.

practiceQuestions.title: The clockmaker's workshop
practiceQuestions.passage:
The following text is from an original short story. Ilse has returned to the workshop where her late aunt repaired clocks.

The bench was as she had left it, which is to say as her aunt had left it: loupe, tweezers, a saucer of screws sorted by a logic Ilse had never been taught. She had expected the room to accuse her of something—of the years she had stayed away, perhaps. Instead it merely continued. A mantel clock on the shelf, gutted and waiting, seemed less a reproach than an invitation that did not much care whether it was accepted.
practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Ilse decides to finish the clock repair that her aunt was unable to complete.
Ilse regrets that she never learned her aunt's method for organizing tools.
Ilse finds that the workshop meets her with indifference instead of the blame she had expected.
Ilse discovers that the workshop has fallen into disorder since her aunt's death.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ilse expected the room to "accuse her," but "instead it merely continued," and the waiting clock is an invitation that "did not much care" whether she accepted. The text turns on that reversal: indifference where she expected blame.
rationales: This goes too far. The gutted clock is described as an invitation, but nothing says Ilse accepts it or decides to finish the repair.
The screws sorted "by a logic Ilse had never been taught" are a passing detail, and the text never says she regrets it.
Correct. Ilse expected the room to accuse her; instead it "merely continued," and even the clock is an invitation that doesn't care whether she accepts.
This contradicts the text: the bench was "as she had left it," with the screws still sorted.
