ieltsListening.title: Coastal Cycle Tours – Booking a Family Tour
ieltsListening.transcriptHtml:
Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man and an assistant at a company that organises cycle tours. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

Emma: Good morning, Coastal Cycle Tours, Emma speaking. How can I help?

Martin: Oh, hello. I'd like to book one of your family bike tours, if there's still space.

Emma: Certainly. I'll just take a few details. Could I have your name, please?

Martin: Yes, it's Martin Ashworth.

Emma: Could you spell your surname for me?

Martin: Of course. A, S, H, W, O, R, T, H.

Emma: Thank you, Mr Ashworth. And what's the best number to contact you on?

Martin: My mobile, please. It's oh seven nine one five, three four six, eight oh two.

Emma: Oh seven nine one five, three four six, eight oh two. Lovely. Now, which tour were you interested in?

Martin: We were hoping to do the Castle Trail. A friend of ours did it last summer and loved it.

Emma: Ah, I'm afraid the Castle Trail is fully booked for the next two months. It's very popular with schools. But the Lighthouse Trail is about the same length, and it follows the cliffs, so the views are wonderful.

Martin: The Lighthouse Trail. Yes, let's do that one instead.

Emma: Great. And which date would you like?

Martin: We were thinking of Saturday the twelfth of July.

Emma: Let me check. Hmm, the twelfth is full, I'm afraid, but there are places on Saturday the nineteenth.

Martin: The nineteenth is fine. We're here for the whole month.

Emma: Perfect. And how many people will be in the group?

Martin: It'll be me and my wife, plus our children. We've got three. My brother might come too, but he isn't sure yet, so let's just say the five of us for now.

Emma: So two adults and three children. Will any of the children need anything special?

Martin: Well, our youngest is only three, so she can't ride on her own. Do you have child seats?

Emma: Yes, we can fit a child seat to one of the adult bikes. I'll add that to the booking.

Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

Emma: Now, let me give you some information about the day itself. The tour leaves from the car park behind the aquarium.

Martin: Not the big car park by the beach?

Emma: No, that one gets very busy in summer. It's the smaller one behind the aquarium, on Harbour Street.

Martin: Right. And what time do we need to be there?

Emma: The tour itself starts at nine thirty, but please arrive about fifteen minutes early so we can check the bikes and adjust the seats.

Martin: Nine thirty. Okay. Is there anything we should bring?

Emma: We provide helmets and bike locks for everyone, and there's a cafe stop halfway, so you don't need to bring food. But you'll need to bring your own gloves. The handlebars can get quite slippery if it rains.

Martin: Gloves. I'll make sure the children have some. And how much will it cost altogether?

Emma: Adults are thirty pounds each and children are twelve, and there's no charge for the child seat. So that comes to ninety-six pounds in total.

Martin: That's fine. Can I pay now?

Emma: Of course. I'll just need your card details.

That is the end of part one.

ieltsListening.title: Maple Hill Library – Changes During Renovation
ieltsListening.transcriptHtml:
Part two. You will hear the manager of a public library talking to local residents about changes to the library. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

David Reid: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name's David Reid, and I've been the manager of Maple Hill Library for six years. As many of you know, the library will be closing for renovation next month, and I'd like to explain what's happening and what it means for you.

David Reid: First of all, why are we doing this? A lot of people have assumed that we're running out of room for books, but in fact we'll have slightly fewer shelves when we reopen, not more. The new heating system should also cut our energy bills, which is welcome, but that isn't the main reason either. The real purpose of the work is to create spaces where people can study and work together, because at the moment we simply don't have anywhere for groups to meet.

David Reid: While the building is closed, you'll still be able to borrow books. We had planned to set up a temporary library in the town hall, but unfortunately the town hall has had problems with its roof, so we've moved the temporary collection to the sports centre on Park Road. The mobile library will also carry on visiting the villages as usual.

David Reid: Now, when will we reopen? Our original plan was to reopen in early March. However, the new heating system won't be delivered until February, so we now expect to open our doors again in late April. We'll post the exact date on our website as soon as we know it.

David Reid: Some of you have asked about library cards. Your existing card will still work after the renovation, so there's no need to replace it. What's new is that you'll also be able to borrow books using an app on your phone, if you prefer. And I'm pleased to say that membership will remain completely free.

David Reid: Finally, we'd like your help. We can't accept donations of books at the moment, because we have nowhere to store them, and the move itself is being handled by a professional company. But the new building will have three meeting rooms, and we'd love you to suggest names for them. There's a box by the door where you can leave your ideas.

Now look at questions sixteen to twenty. You have some time to read them.

Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

David Reid: Now let me go through some of the specific services and how they'll change. We're adding four new study rooms. They'll be very popular, so you'll need to reserve one in advance, either online or at the desk. You won't be able to just turn up and use them.

David Reid: Next, the computer area. At the moment we charge one pound an hour for the computers, and a lot of you have told us that this is unfair. So from April, using the computers will be free for all members. We'll also have twice as many machines.

David Reid: The children's section has always been on the ground floor, next to the entrance, and it can get quite noisy for everyone else. So in the new building it will be on the first floor, where there's more space and a separate reading area for toddlers.

David Reid: Many of you enjoy the cafe. It will stay open in the same place, but from now on it will be run by a group of volunteers from the Friends of Maple Hill Library, rather than by an outside company. Any profits will go towards buying new books.

David Reid: And the local history room, which has old maps, newspapers and photographs of the area, is currently only open on weekday mornings. After the renovation it will stay open until eight o'clock on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, so that people who work during the day can use it too.

David Reid: One service that won't be returning, I'm afraid, is photocopying, which has hardly been used since everyone started taking pictures of documents with their phones. Right, are there any questions?

That is the end of part two.

ieltsListening.title: Student Project on Canteen Food Waste
ieltsListening.transcriptHtml:
Part three. You will hear two students, Anna and Kieran, discussing a research project on food waste in their university canteen. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-four.

Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-four.

Anna: So, Kieran, have you had a chance to look at the results from the canteen survey?

Kieran: I have. Some of it was what we expected. The kitchen staff do throw away quite a lot of food at the end of each day, but we knew that before we started.

Anna: True. What really surprised me was what was being thrown away. I was sure meat would be the biggest problem, because it's the most expensive.

Kieran: Me too. But vegetables made up almost half of all the waste. Especially the side dishes. People take them and then leave them on the plate.

Anna: And the other thing I didn't expect was the timing. I assumed dinner would be worse, because people are tired and take too much, but actually far more food was wasted at lunchtime.

Kieran: Probably because everyone's in a hurry to get to afternoon lectures. What about bread? I thought students would leave a lot of bread.

Anna: No, hardly any. And the portions were about the size we'd predicted, so nothing unusual there.

Kieran: So then we met the canteen manager. What did you think of her reaction?

Anna: She was more positive than I thought she'd be. She agreed to try taking away the trays for a month. The idea is that without a tray, people can't pile up so many dishes.

Kieran: Yes, and she liked the idea of half portions, too. She said she'd offer smaller portions at a lower price as a trial.

Anna: She wasn't keen on the posters, though.

Kieran: No, she said they put posters up last year and nobody paid any attention. And she pointed out that they already give leftover food to a local charity, so that's not really something new.

Anna: And changing the menu every day just isn't possible with the staff they have.

Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions twenty-five to thirty.

Now listen and answer questions twenty-five to thirty.

Anna: Right, we need to divide up the rest of the work. We'll need another meeting with the manager at the end of the trial.

Kieran: I can arrange that. I've got her email address, and I'm in the canteen most days anyway.

Anna: Great. Then there are all the photographs of the plates we took. Someone has to go through them and sort them into categories.

Kieran: That's a big job.

Anna: I don't mind doing it. I took most of them, so I know what's there.

Kieran: Thanks. What about the other universities? Our tutor said we should look at studies from other places.

Anna: There's quite a lot of material. I think we should both read some of it, and then compare notes.

Kieran: Agreed. I'll do the graphs, then. I enjoy that kind of thing, and I've already put the survey data into a spreadsheet.

Anna: Perfect. And I'll write the introduction, since I wrote the original proposal.

Kieran: Okay. And the handout for the presentation?

Anna: Let's do that together at the end, when we know exactly what we're going to say.

Kieran: Good idea.

That is the end of part three.

ieltsListening.title: Lecture: Why Roman Concrete Has Lasted
ieltsListening.transcriptHtml:
Part four. You will hear a lecture about the concrete used in ancient Rome. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

Lecturer: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a material that most of us walk past every day without noticing: concrete. And in particular, I want to look at why some concrete built by the ancient Romans has lasted for around two thousand years, while a lot of modern concrete starts to crack and crumble within a few decades.

Lecturer: Let's start with some examples. Roman harbours built in the sea are still standing today, which is remarkable, because salt water is extremely damaging to most building materials. And in Rome itself, the Pantheon is topped by a huge dome made of concrete with no steel inside it. Nearly two thousand years after it was built, it is still the largest dome of its kind in the world.

Lecturer: So what was the Romans' secret? The basic recipe was lime mixed with volcanic ash, which they collected from areas around the Bay of Naples. This ash reacts with lime to create a very strong binding material. In their sea walls, something even more interesting happened. Over many years, seawater seeping into the concrete reacted with the ash and caused new crystals to grow inside it. So instead of wearing the walls away, the sea actually made the material stronger over time.

Lecturer: Another puzzle was the small white lumps that are found in almost all Roman concrete. These are lumps of lime, and for a long time researchers assumed they were simply a sign of careless mixing, or of poor-quality ingredients. But a study published in twenty twenty-three suggested a very different explanation.

Lecturer: The researchers believe that the Romans used a technique now called hot mixing. Instead of mixing the lime with water first, builders added it in a highly reactive form known as quicklime. This produces a great deal of heat, and the heat changes the chemistry of the mixture in useful ways. Crucially, it leaves behind those lumps of lime. Then, when a small crack appears and water gets in, the lime in the lumps dissolves and then hardens again, filling the gap. In other words, the concrete can repair itself, and this stops cracks from spreading through the structure.

Lecturer: Why does any of this matter today? Well, the production of cement, the key ingredient in modern concrete, is responsible for around eight per cent of the world's carbon emissions. If we could build structures that last much longer, we would need to replace them less often, and a Roman-style mix could also need far less maintenance during its lifetime.

Lecturer: However, we shouldn't assume that Roman concrete is better in every way. It is not as strong as modern concrete under very heavy loads, and it also sets much more slowly, which would make construction projects take longer. So engineers are not trying to copy the Romans exactly. Instead, they are looking for ways to give modern concrete the same ability to heal itself. In the next part of the lecture, I'll look at some of these experiments.

That is the end of part four.

ieltsReading.title: The Hidden Lives of Reef Fish
ieltsReading.contentHtml:
For decades, scientists who study coral reefs focused mainly on the corals themselves: how they grow, how they reproduce and why they die. The fish that swim among them were often treated as little more than decoration. Over the past thirty years, however, marine biologists have discovered that reef fish play a far more active role in keeping reefs healthy than anyone had imagined.

One of the most important of these roles is grazing. Many reef fish, particularly parrotfish and surgeonfish, feed on the algae that grow on dead coral. Without them, fast-growing algae can quickly cover a reef and prevent young corals from settling. In a well-known experiment in the Caribbean, researchers fenced off small areas of reef so that grazing fish could not enter. Within a year, algae covered almost ninety per cent of the protected areas, compared with less than twenty per cent of the areas outside the fences.

Parrotfish have another surprising effect on their environment. As they scrape algae from rock, they also swallow small pieces of coral skeleton, which they grind into fine sand and excrete. A single large parrotfish can produce several hundred kilograms of sand each year, and some of the white beaches that attract tourists to tropical islands are made largely of this material.

Reef fish are also more intelligent than was once believed. The cleaner wrasse, a small blue-and-black fish, runs what biologists describe as 'cleaning stations', where larger fish come to have parasites removed from their skin and gills. Studies have shown that cleaner wrasse remember individual clients and treat them differently: they are more careful with fish that have other stations nearby, since these customers could easily go elsewhere. In laboratory tests, cleaner wrasse have even passed a version of the mirror test, which is often used to measure self-awareness in animals.

Size, too, matters in unexpected ways. It has long been assumed that bigger fish are more likely to survive attacks by predators, because they can swim faster and are harder to swallow. A study carried out at Lizard Island, on Australia's Great Barrier Reef, challenged this idea. Researchers tagged young damselfish of different sizes and followed them for several weeks. Surprisingly, larger individuals were not more likely to survive. Instead, survival depended mainly on the fish's position on the reef and the amount of shelter available, suggesting that choosing a good hiding place matters more than growing quickly.

Studying reef fish in the wild is far from easy. Many species are active only at night, and the complex structure of a reef makes it difficult to follow individual animals. Traditional methods, such as counting fish while swimming along a measured line, depend heavily on the experience of the diver and can disturb shy species. For this reason, researchers increasingly rely on underwater cameras, which can record behaviour for many hours without a human present.

These studies have become more urgent as reefs face growing threats. Rising sea temperatures cause corals to lose the algae that live inside them, a process known as bleaching. When a reef bleaches, the fish that depend on it for food and shelter often disappear within months. Some scientists argue that protecting populations of grazing fish may give damaged reefs a better chance of recovering, and several countries have already banned the fishing of parrotfish for this reason.

ieltsReading.title: Can Eating Less Help Us Live Longer?
ieltsReading.contentHtml:
A  In the 1930s, a nutrition scientist at Cornell University named Clive McCay made a curious discovery. Rats that were fed a diet containing all the necessary nutrients, but around a third fewer calories than normal, lived considerably longer than rats that could eat as much as they liked. Some of the underfed rats lived almost twice as long as the others. At the time, the finding attracted little interest outside the laboratory, and it would be several decades before other scientists took it seriously.

B  Since then, the same effect has been observed in a remarkable range of species, from yeast and worms to fruit flies and mice. In most cases, reducing food intake by between twenty and forty per cent extends average lifespan, and animals on restricted diets also tend to develop age-related diseases such as cancer later in life. The consistency of these results has led some researchers to describe calorie restriction as the most reliable way known to slow ageing in laboratory animals.

C  Exactly why eating less should have this effect is still debated. One early theory held that a slower metabolism simply meant less 'wear and tear' on the body. More recent work points to changes inside cells. When food is scarce, cells appear to switch from growth to maintenance, repairing damaged proteins and recycling worn-out components in a process called autophagy. A group of genes that respond to nutrient levels seems to control this switch, and several of them have been found in almost all animals, including humans.

D  Whether these findings apply to people is much harder to establish. Human lives are long, and few volunteers are willing to eat far less than they want for decades. The largest controlled trial so far, known as CALERIE, asked healthy adults to reduce their calorie intake by a quarter for two years. In practice, most participants managed a reduction of only about twelve per cent. Even so, they showed improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol and other markers linked to heart disease.

E  Two well-known studies of monkeys produced conflicting results. In one, carried out at the University of Wisconsin, monkeys on a restricted diet lived longer and suffered less disease than a control group. In the other, at the National Institute on Aging, restriction brought health benefits but no clear increase in lifespan. Researchers later pointed out that the control monkeys in the second study had themselves been fed a fairly limited, healthy diet, which may explain why the difference between the two groups was small.

F  Because strict calorie restriction is so difficult, attention has turned to alternatives that might produce similar benefits. These include intermittent fasting, in which people eat normally on most days but very little on one or two days a week, and drugs that imitate the effects of food shortage on cells. Early results are encouraging, but most scientists warn that eating too little can be harmful, particularly for older people, who need enough protein to maintain muscle strength.

ieltsReading.title: What Makes an Expert Musician?
ieltsReading.contentHtml:
It is often said that it takes ten thousand hours of practice to become an expert in any field. The figure became famous after the publication of a popular book in 2008, which drew on research carried out in the early 1990s by the psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues. In their study, violin students at a music academy in Berlin were divided into three groups according to their teachers' judgements of their ability. The researchers then asked the students to estimate how much time they had spent practising since they first picked up the instrument. By the age of twenty, the best violinists had accumulated an average of around ten thousand hours of practice, while the least accomplished group had practised for about four thousand hours.

Ericsson did not claim that ten thousand hours was a magic number, and he was frustrated by the way his work was later described. What mattered, he argued, was not simply the quantity of practice but its quality. He used the term 'deliberate practice' to describe activity that is specifically designed to improve performance: it is usually guided by a teacher, focuses on weaknesses rather than strengths, and involves constant feedback. Playing through a favourite piece for enjoyment, however pleasant, does not count.

In recent years, several researchers have questioned whether practice alone can explain expert performance. In 2014, a team led by Brooke Macnamara combined the results of dozens of earlier studies and concluded that deliberate practice accounted for only about a fifth of the differences in musical skill between individuals. Other factors, they suggested, must also play a significant role. One of these may be the age at which training begins. Children who start music lessons early seem to have an advantage that is not fully explained by the extra hours of practice they accumulate, perhaps because the developing brain is especially flexible.

Genetics is another candidate. A large study of Swedish twins found that identical twins, who share all of their genes, were more similar in their musical ability than non-identical twins, even when one twin had practised far more than the other. The researchers were careful to point out that this does not mean practice is pointless – the twin who practised more was usually the better player – but it does suggest that people differ in how much they benefit from it.

Personality may matter too. Psychologists have found that people who score highly on a trait called 'openness to experience', which includes curiosity and an interest in art, are more likely to take up an instrument and to persist with it. Motivation is equally important. Practice, particularly the deliberate kind, is often tiring and not always enjoyable, and learners who are driven by a genuine love of music tend to continue for longer than those who are pushed by parents or teachers.

Finally, some researchers emphasise the role of the environment in which a musician grows up. Access to good teachers, instruments and opportunities to perform is far from equally distributed, and a gifted child in a family without these resources may never discover his or her potential. From this point of view, expertise is not only a matter of individual effort or talent, but also of opportunity.

Most researchers now accept that expert musicianship is the product of many interacting factors. The debate is no longer about whether practice or talent matters, but about how the two combine. For teachers, this suggests that encouraging practice remains essential, but that it should be designed carefully and adapted to the individual learner.

ieltsReading.title: The Return of the Urban Fox
ieltsReading.contentHtml:
A  For most of the twentieth century, the red fox was regarded in Britain as a creature of the countryside, hunted by farmers who blamed it for killing chickens and young lambs. Yet from the 1930s onwards, a small number of foxes began to appear in the suburbs of London and other southern cities. Today, it is estimated that around 150,000 foxes live in British towns and cities, and many residents see one more often than they see a hedgehog.

B  The first urban foxes probably moved into the new suburbs that spread rapidly between the two world wars. These areas, with their large gardens, quiet railway lines and low-density housing, offered plenty of places to hide and raise young. Unlike the crowded city centres, they also provided a rich supply of food, from fruit trees and bird tables to insects and earthworms in lawns.

C  Contrary to popular belief, urban foxes do not rely mainly on rubbish bins. When researchers at the University of Bristol analysed the diet of foxes killed on roads, they found that around a third of it consisted of food deliberately left out by people, while the rest was made up of animals the foxes had caught themselves, such as rats, pigeons and beetles, together with fruit and animals found dead by the road.

D  City life has changed fox behaviour in several ways. Urban foxes tend to have smaller territories than their rural relatives, sometimes covering no more than a few streets, because food is so concentrated. They have also become bolder: studies using cameras have shown that city foxes approach unfamiliar objects more quickly than country foxes, which may help them to exploit new sources of food.

E  Not everyone welcomes the animals. Complaints about foxes digging in gardens, screaming at night during the breeding season and occasionally entering houses are common. Some local councils receive hundreds of calls about foxes every year, yet experts argue that removing the animals is pointless, because any territory that becomes empty is quickly filled by a fox from a neighbouring area.

F  Instead, wildlife organisations recommend that people learn to live alongside foxes. Simple measures, such as keeping rubbish in sealed containers, blocking gaps under sheds and never feeding foxes by hand, can greatly reduce problems. Some researchers believe that urban foxes may even be useful, since they help to control the populations of rats and mice.

ieltsReading.title: The Story of the Tin Can
ieltsReading.contentHtml:
Today, the tin can is so ordinary that it is easy to forget it was once a revolutionary invention. Its story begins not in a factory but on the battlefield. In 1795, France was at war with much of Europe, and its armies were struggling to feed soldiers who were fighting far from home. Fresh food spoiled quickly, and the salted and dried food that soldiers carried was often unpleasant and lacking in nutrients. The French government therefore offered a large cash prize to anyone who could find a better way of preserving food for its troops.

The challenge was taken up by Nicolas Appert, a confectioner from Paris. Over roughly fourteen years of experiments, Appert developed a method in which food was placed in thick glass bottles, sealed with cork and wax, and then heated in boiling water. Food prepared in this way stayed fresh for months, and samples that were sent to sea with the French navy were found to be in excellent condition when the ships returned. In 1810, Appert received the prize of 12,000 francs, on the condition that he publish a description of his method, which he did in a book the same year.

What Appert could not explain was why his method worked. He believed that the heat somehow drove out the air, and that air was responsible for food going bad. It was not until the 1860s that the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that spoilage is caused by microorganisms, and that heating food kills them. Appert had found the right answer for the wrong reason.

Glass had one serious disadvantage: it broke easily, particularly when it was carried in army supply wagons over rough roads. In the same year that Appert won his prize, a British merchant called Peter Durand was granted a patent for preserving food in containers made of iron coated with tin. Durand does not appear to have manufactured any cans himself. Instead, he sold his patent to two engineers, Bryan Donkin and John Hall, who set up a factory in London. By 1813 they were supplying tinned meat and vegetables to the Royal Navy, and the Duke of Wellington is said to have tasted their products and approved of them.

Early cans were a far cry from the light containers we know today. They were made by hand, with a skilled worker producing only a few dozen a day, and they were so heavy that some weighed more than the food inside them. Opening them was not easy either. Instructions printed on some early cans advised the user to cut around the top with a chisel and hammer. Remarkably, the first tool designed specifically for opening cans did not appear until 1855, more than forty years after the first cans were sold. Invented in England by Robert Yeates, it was a lever with a claw at one end, which was pushed into the lid and worked around the edge. The design that most people would recognise, which uses a sharp wheel that rolls around the rim, was patented in the United States by William Lyman in 1870.

By then, canned food had become part of everyday life. During the American Civil War in the 1860s, soldiers on both sides depended on it, and many of them continued to buy canned goods after returning home. Factories introduced machines that made cans faster and more cheaply, and as cans became thinner, opening them became much easier.

The history of the can also includes some darker episodes. In 1845, the British explorer Sir John Franklin set off to find a sea route through the Arctic with two ships and a large supply of tinned food. None of the 129 men returned. Examinations of remains found many years later showed high levels of lead, and some researchers have suggested that the solder used to seal the cans, which contained lead, contributed to the men's illness. Others argue that the ships' water systems were a more likely source, and the question is still debated.

In the twentieth century, the can continued to evolve. Aluminium, which is lighter than steel and does not rust, became the standard material for drinks cans in the 1960s, and the ring pull meant that no tool was needed at all. More than two hundred years after Appert's first experiments, the basic principle he discovered – heating food in a sealed container – remains at the heart of the canning industry.

ieltsReading.title: Cooling the Urban Heat Island
ieltsReading.contentHtml:
A  On a summer night in a large city, the air can be several degrees warmer than in the surrounding countryside. This phenomenon, now known as the urban heat island, was first described more than two hundred years ago. In the early nineteenth century, an amateur scientist named Luke Howard recorded temperatures in London and in the fields outside it, and noticed that the city was consistently warmer, especially at night. His findings attracted little attention at the time, but today the urban heat island is one of the most intensively studied features of city climates, and differences of up to ten degrees Celsius between urban and rural areas have been recorded on calm, clear nights.

B  The causes of this extra warmth are well understood. Dark surfaces such as roads and roofs absorb a large proportion of the sunlight that falls on them and release the heat slowly after sunset. Tall buildings trap this heat and block the winds that might otherwise carry it away, while the lack of soil and vegetation means that there is little water available to cool the air through evaporation. On top of this, cities produce heat of their own: every car engine, factory and air-conditioning unit releases warmth into the surrounding streets.

C  It would be easy to regard the heat island as nothing more than an inconvenience, but its effects can be serious. During heatwaves, high night-time temperatures prevent people's bodies from recovering from the heat of the day, and the elderly and those with health conditions are particularly at risk. Hotter cities also consume more electricity, as residents turn up their air conditioning. Because much of that electricity is still generated by burning fossil fuels, and because air conditioners themselves pump hot air into the street, the result is a vicious circle in which attempts to stay cool make the city warmer still. Higher temperatures also speed up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, a harmful air pollutant.

D  One of the simplest ways to cool a city is to change the colour of its surfaces. Light-coloured materials reflect more sunlight and therefore absorb less heat, and so-called 'cool roofs', painted white or covered with reflective coatings, can be many degrees cooler than traditional dark roofs on a sunny day. Several cities have also experimented with reflective coatings on roads. In Los Angeles, where some streets were coated with a pale grey material, measurements showed a significant fall in the temperature of the road surface. However, researchers have warned that reflective pavements may bounce sunlight back onto people walking on them, so that pedestrians feel hotter even though the road itself is cooler.

E  Plants offer another solution. Trees cool the air in two ways: they provide shade, and they release water vapour through their leaves, a process that absorbs heat from their surroundings. Studies have found that large parks can be several degrees cooler than nearby streets, and even a single row of trees can make a noticeable difference. For this reason, many cities have set ambitious targets for tree planting. Melbourne, for example, aims to increase the proportion of the city covered by tree canopy to forty per cent by 2040. Yet trees are not a simple fix. They need a reliable supply of water, which may be scarce during the very heatwaves they are meant to protect against, and in crowded city centres there is often too little space for their roots to grow.

F  Increasingly, researchers are turning their attention to who suffers most from urban heat. Satellite images and networks of inexpensive temperature sensors have revealed that heat is not evenly distributed within cities. In many places, the hottest neighbourhoods are those with the fewest trees and the most concrete, and these are frequently the areas where people on low incomes live. Some of these residents cannot afford air conditioning, or the electricity to run it. Planners are therefore being urged to consider not only how much a city can be cooled, but where cooling measures are most needed.

ieltsReading.title: In Praise of Boredom
ieltsReading.contentHtml:
Boredom has a bad reputation. It is blamed for everything from mindless snacking and reckless driving to vandalism, and surveys regularly find that it is one of the emotions people most want to avoid. Parents worry when their children complain of having nothing to do, and employers fear that bored staff will make careless mistakes. It is hardly surprising, then, that so much ingenuity has gone into making sure we never have to experience it.

Yet it is worth asking what boredom actually is. One widely cited definition, proposed by the psychologist John Eastwood and his colleagues, describes it as the uncomfortable experience of wanting to engage in satisfying activity but being unable to do so. Crucially, on this view, boredom is not the same as having nothing to do. A person can be very busy and still bored, if what they are doing fails to hold their attention; equally, someone with empty hours ahead may feel perfectly content.

What has changed in recent years is how easily boredom can be escaped. With a smartphone in almost every pocket, a moment of emptiness can be filled instantly with messages, videos or news. The effect, I would argue, is not that we are less bored, but that we have lost the habit of tolerating even brief periods without stimulation. A striking illustration comes from a series of experiments published in 2014 by Timothy Wilson of the University of Virginia. Participants were asked to sit alone in a room with nothing to do but think, for between six and fifteen minutes, and most found the experience unpleasant. In one version of the study, participants were given the option of giving themselves a mild electric shock during the session – a shock that they had earlier said they would pay money to avoid. Remarkably, around two thirds of the men and a quarter of the women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than simply sit with their thoughts.

If boredom is so unpleasant, why might it be worth preserving? One answer comes from research on creativity. In a study carried out by Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman at the University of Central Lancashire, some participants were first given the deliberately dull task of copying numbers from a telephone directory, while others went straight to a creativity test in which they had to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had done the boring task came up with more ideas. In a second experiment, a group who merely read the numbers, rather than writing them down, did better still. This suggests that the less engaging the task, the more the mind was free to wander – and wandering, it seems, is where new ideas come from.

Philosophers have offered a further reason to value boredom. Andreas Elpidorou has argued that boredom works rather like pain: it is unpleasant in itself, but useful as a signal. Just as pain warns us that our body has been damaged, boredom tells us that our current activity no longer matches our goals, and pushes us to look for something more meaningful. On this account, a person who never allows themselves to feel bored may also miss the prompt to change direction.

None of this means that boredom is always harmless. Researchers distinguish between the passing boredom that everyone feels in a traffic jam or a long meeting and a chronic tendency to feel bored, which has been linked with depression, anxiety and problem gambling. For people who experience boredom in this more persistent form, the advice to 'embrace' it would be unhelpful, and in some cases professional support may be needed.

For the rest of us, however, the evidence suggests that our constant efforts to escape boredom may come at a cost. The point is not to seek out tedium for its own sake, nor to deny that some tasks are genuinely dull. Rather, it is that occasional boredom deserves to be tolerated instead of immediately cured. The next time a queue or a delayed train leaves us with nothing to do, it may be worth resisting the urge to reach for our phones, and seeing where our thoughts lead.

ieltsWriting.title: Task 1 – Books read by age group
ieltsWriting.questionHtml:
The chart below shows the average number of books read per person in one year by people in four age groups in a European country, in 2005 and 2025.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
ieltsWriting.modelAnswerHtml:
The bar chart compares how many books people in four age groups read on average in a year in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, reading declined among younger adults over the twenty-year period but increased among older people, so that by 2025 the over-60s had become by far the most active readers.

In 2005, the number of books read rose steadily with age, from nine a year for 16- to 24-year-olds to eleven and twelve for the two middle groups, and fourteen for those aged 60 and over. The gap between the youngest and oldest groups was therefore relatively small.

By 2025, this pattern had become much more pronounced. The two younger groups each read three fewer books than before, at six and eight respectively. In contrast, reading among 40- to 59-year-olds rose slightly, to thirteen books, while the figure for the over-60s increased sharply, by five books to nineteen a year – more than three times the figure for the youngest group.

ieltsWriting.title: Task 1 – How glass bottles are recycled
ieltsWriting.questionHtml:
The diagram below shows how glass bottles are recycled.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.
ieltsWriting.modelAnswerHtml:
The diagram illustrates the process by which used glass bottles are recycled to make new ones.

Overall, the process consists of nine stages, beginning with the collection of old bottles and ending with new bottles returning to shops, so it forms a continuous cycle.

First, used bottles are collected from bottle banks and taken by lorry to a recycling plant. There, they are sorted into three colours – clear, green and brown – before being washed to remove labels and dirt. The clean glass is then crushed into small pieces, known as cullet.

In the next stage, the cullet is mixed with sand and other raw materials, and the mixture is heated in a furnace to around 1,500°C until it melts. The molten glass is poured into moulds and shaped into new bottles. Finally, these bottles are filled and delivered to shops, where they are bought by consumers, and the cycle can begin again.

ieltsWriting.title: Task 2 – Money lessons at school
ieltsWriting.questionHtml:
Some people believe that secondary schools should teach students how to manage money, for example how to budget, save and borrow sensibly. Others think that this is the responsibility of parents, not schools.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
ieltsWriting.modelAnswerHtml:
Many young people leave school with little idea of how to manage a budget or avoid debt. While some argue that teaching these skills is a job for parents, I believe schools are better placed to take the lead, although families still have an important part to play.

Those who think money management belongs at home make a fair point. Attitudes to spending and saving are shaped by everyday family life, as children watch how their parents handle bills or save for holidays. Parents can also tailor their advice to their own circumstances, and some feel that financial matters are a private issue in which the state should not interfere.

However, relying on parents alone has serious drawbacks. Not all adults are confident with money themselves, and those who have struggled with debt may pass on the same habits without realising it. If financial education happens only at home, children from less stable backgrounds are likely to be at a disadvantage. A school course, by contrast, would give every student the same basic knowledge, such as how interest on a loan works or how to plan a monthly budget. It could also use practical activities, such as managing an imaginary salary, which make abstract ideas easier to understand.

In my view, schools should therefore teach the fundamentals of personal finance to all students, ideally as a compulsory part of the curriculum in the final years of secondary education. Parents can then build on these lessons by discussing real decisions with their children.

In conclusion, although families influence how young people think about money, schools offer the fairest and most reliable way to make sure that everyone leaves education with the skills they need to manage their finances.

ieltsWriting.title: Task 2 – Young people leaving rural areas
ieltsWriting.questionHtml:
In many countries, young people are leaving the countryside to live and work in cities.

Why is this happening? What can be done to make rural areas more attractive to young people?
ieltsWriting.modelAnswerHtml:
In many countries, young people are moving away from villages and small towns in large numbers. This essay will examine the main reasons for this trend and suggest some measures that could make rural life more appealing.

The most important cause is the shortage of good jobs outside cities. Agriculture, traditionally the main employer in the countryside, now relies heavily on machinery and needs far fewer workers, while most well-paid positions in areas such as technology and finance are concentrated in urban centres. Education is a second factor. Universities and colleges are usually located in cities, and young people who move there to study often build their careers and social lives there too. Finally, many young adults are attracted by the wider range of entertainment, services and cultural activities that cities offer.

Governments could reduce this movement in several ways. First, they could encourage businesses to open offices in rural areas by offering tax incentives, and invest in fast internet connections so that people can work remotely for city-based companies. Second, improving transport links would allow young people to live in the countryside while still having access to urban jobs and facilities. Local authorities could also support community projects, such as sports clubs, festivals and shared workspaces, which give young residents a reason to stay and a sense of belonging.

In conclusion, young people leave rural areas mainly because of limited job and study opportunities and a lack of amenities. Although this trend is unlikely to be reversed completely, better connectivity, transport and investment in local communities could make the countryside a far more attractive place to build a life.

Task 2 – Money lessons at school
ieltsPracticeAttempts.essay:
Many people argue that teaching young people how to handle money is a job for families, while others believe that secondary schools should take on this role. In my view, although parents have an important part to play, schools are better placed to make sure that every student learns these skills.

On the one hand, there are good reasons to leave financial education to parents. Money habits are formed at home, where children watch how adults shop, save and pay bills. Parents can also give practical advice that fits their own family's situation, for example by helping a teenager open a first bank account.

On the other hand, not all parents are confident with money themselves, and some may pass on poor habits such as relying on credit cards. If financial education depends entirely on families, students from these homes will be at a disadvantage. Schools, however, can offer the same lessons to everyone. Moreover, teachers can explain topics like interest rates and loans in a structured way, and link them to mathematics lessons.

Furthermore, the consequences of poor money management can be serious. Many young adults fall into debt soon after leaving school because they do not understand how borrowing works. A short course in budgeting and saving could prevent many of these problems.

In conclusion, while parents should certainly talk to their children about money, I believe that secondary schools should be responsible for teaching the basic skills, because this is the only way to ensure that all young people receive this important knowledge.
